dicas.texto: Boa observação! Quando o problema diz '30 minutos ou 2/4 de uma hora', qual parte representa o número de partes que estamos usando? E qual representa o total de partes iguais em uma hora?

Continue assim! Localize no texto onde aparece a fração escrita. O numerador é o número de cima (partes usadas), e o denominador é o de baixo (total de partes na unidade). Digite-os nos campos corretos.
Quase lá! A fração está escrita exatamente como '2/4' no enunciado. Você não precisa mudá-la — só identificá-la. Confira: quantas partes da hora ela usou? Em quantas partes a hora foi dividida?
Você está muito perto! O enunciado diz claramente '2/4 de uma hora'. Então, o número de cima (numerador) é 2, e o de baixo (denominador) é 4. Digite esses números nas caixas correspondentes.
Ótima dúvida! Se a unidade (de 0 a 1) for dividida em 4 partes iguais, onde ficaria a segunda parte? Pense: cada parte é um quarto — onde termina o segundo quarto?
Você está no caminho certo! Divida mentalmente a reta em 4 partes iguais. Comece em 0, depois o primeiro ponto é 1/4, o segundo é 2/4. Marque exatamente nesse segundo ponto.
Quase lá! A reta tem encaixe automático em quartos, mesmo com marcas ocultas. Arraste o ponto até sentir o 'clique' no meio da reta — isso corresponde a 2/4.
Muito bem! 2/4 fica exatamente na metade entre 0 e 1. Mova o ponto até o centro da reta — você verá que ele se encaixa perfeitamente lá.

Select two parts in the model so the top number represents the selected fourths.
The denominator describes how the whole hour was divided.
Count all equal sections in the fraction model, not only the selected sections.

Read the fraction from top to bottom and place the first number in f1.

A fraction on a number line shows how far we move from zero toward one whole.
Use the denominator to count the equal intervals and the numerator to count the intervals from zero.

Start at 0, move across two of the four equal intervals, and place the point there.
Compare the numerator with the denominator to decide whether the fraction contains a complete whole.

In m1, enter the count of complete wholes formed by the available fourths.

Sarah parked her car at a parking meter. To park for 15 minutes, or 1/4 of an hour, it cost a quarter. Sarah had to park for 30 minutes or 2/4 of an hour. Show 2/4 on the number line.

Exercicio completo
Read the parking story and enter the numerator of Sarah's fraction in the top box.
nodes.instruction: Read the parking story and enter the numerator of Sarah's fraction in the top box.

hints.message: Look for the fraction that describes Sarah's own parking time, not the example for 15 minutes.
In a fraction, read the number above the fraction bar first.
The fraction for 30 minutes is written as 2/4 in the story.
Click the top box and enter the number that appears before the slash in Sarah's fraction.

misconceptions.description: Aluno foca no exemplo inicial e responde com 1/4, ignorando que a pergunta é sobre o segundo cenário.
misconceptions.feedback: You used the numerator from the 15-minute example. Sarah parked for 30 minutes, so use the fraction written for her time.

misconceptions.description: Aluno entende que a hora está dividida em 4 partes, mas pensa que o numerador deve ser o número absoluto de minutos.
misconceptions.feedback: The numerator counts fourths of an hour, not minutes. The story says that 30 minutes corresponds to two fourths.

nodes.description: Use the fraction model to identify the top number in 2/4.
nodes.instruction: Use the fraction model to identify the top number in 2/4.

hints.message: The numerator tells how many equal parts are being considered.
Find the number of selected parts in the fraction model, then compare it with the number above the slash.
Two of the four equal parts represent Sarah's parking time.
Select two parts in the model so the top number represents the selected fourths.

misconceptions.description: Aluno lê '2/4' no texto, mas digita o recíproco por confusão na estrutura da fração.
misconceptions.feedback: The 4 tells how many equal parts make one hour, so it belongs below the fraction bar. The top number is the number of selected parts.

nodes.description: Use the fraction model to identify the bottom number in 2/4.
nodes.instruction: Use the fraction model to identify the bottom number in 2/4.

hints.message: The denominator describes how the whole hour was divided.
Count all equal sections in the fraction model, not only the selected sections.
The hour is divided into fourths, so the model has four equal sections.
Select the bottom box and enter the total number of equal parts in one whole hour.

misconceptions.description: Aluno entende que a hora está dividida em 4 partes, mas pensa que o numerador deve ser o número absoluto de minutos.
misconceptions.feedback: The denominator counts equal parts of an hour, not minutes. One hour is divided into four fourths.

nodes.description: Enter the numerator for Sarah's fraction in field f1.
nodes.instruction: Enter the numerator for Sarah's fraction in field f1.

hints.message: The top field records how many fourths Sarah used.
Read the fraction from top to bottom and place the first number in f1.
Sarah used two fourths of an hour.
Click f1 and type the count of fourths used by Sarah.

nodes.description: Enter the denominator in field f2.
nodes.instruction: Enter the denominator in field f2.

hints.message: The bottom field tells how many equal parts make one whole hour.
Use the total number of equal fourths as the denominator.
The story names the fraction as 2/4, so the bottom number is the number after the slash.
Click f2 and type the total number of equal parts in the hour.

nodes.description: Mark 2/4 on the number line from 0 to 1.
nodes.instruction: Mark 2/4 on the number line from 0 to 1.

hints.message: A fraction on a number line shows how far we move from zero toward one whole.
Use the denominator to count the equal intervals and the numerator to count the intervals from zero.
The line has four equal intervals, and Sarah's point is two intervals from zero.
Start at 0, move across two of the four equal intervals, and place the point there.

misconceptions.description: Aluno comete erro de off-by-one ao contar as posições fracionárias na reta.
misconceptions.feedback: You stopped after one interval. Starting at 0, the first mark is 1/4 and the second mark is 2/4.

misconceptions.description: Aluno ignora que a unidade é [0,1] e que há 4 subdivisões; pensa que cada traço = 1.
misconceptions.feedback: Each interval is one fourth of the whole, not one entire unit. The line goes only from 0 to 1.

misconceptions.description: Aluno associa 30 minutos diretamente à metade da reta, ignorando a escala fracionária ou a fração específica.
misconceptions.feedback: The midpoint is equivalent to 2/4, but this task asks you to mark the position represented by the fraction 2/4 using the four-part scale.

nodes.description: Convert the proper fraction to the mixed-number view without changing its value.
nodes.instruction: Convert the proper fraction to the mixed-number view without changing its value.

hints.message: Compare the numerator with the denominator to decide whether the fraction contains a complete whole.
For a proper fraction, identify the number of complete wholes before recording the remaining fractional part.
Two fourths is not enough to make four fourths, which would be one whole.
Use the Convert control and keep the fractional part unchanged while recording the number of complete wholes.

misconceptions.description: Aluno aplica simplificação desnecessária, alterando a forma da fração solicitada.
misconceptions.feedback: 1/2 has the same value, but the requested fraction is written as 2/4. Convert the representation without replacing the given fraction.

nodes.description: Enter the whole-number part of the mixed-number form in field m1.
nodes.instruction: Enter the whole-number part of the mixed-number form in field m1.

hints.message: A mixed number begins with the number of complete wholes.
Compare the numerator and denominator to determine how many complete groups of the denominator fit in the numerator.
The numerator has fewer fourths than are needed for one complete whole.
In m1, enter the count of complete wholes formed by the available fourths.

misconceptions.description: Aluno pressupõe que toda fração deve ser convertida, mesmo sendo própria.
misconceptions.feedback: The numerator counts the remaining fourths, not complete wholes. Since two fourths is less than four fourths, there is no complete whole.
